evals.prompt: We're a small early-stage store just getting started. Let's build a full points program with tiers, multipliers, and a paid membership tier all at once.
evals.expected_output: Should push back on starting with a complex hybrid program, recommending starting simple (a punch card or basic points program) and adding complexity only once the simpler version is proven working. Should explain that a simple program customers understand beats a complex one nobody understands.
assertions: Pushes back on launching a complex multi-mechanic program from day one
Recommends starting with a simpler program type
Does not simply design the full complex program as requested

evals.prompt: We want to launch a subscribe-and-save program for an unpredictable, one-off purchase category (custom furniture).
evals.expected_output: Should flag that subscription commerce only fits consumable, replenishable products with a real predictable usage cycle, and that forcing it onto a one-off or unpredictable-cadence category creates friction without retention benefit. Should recommend against this specific application or ask what genuine recurring need it would actually serve.
assertions: Flags that subscription models don't fit unpredictable, one-off purchase categories
Questions or pushes back on this specific application
Does not simply proceed with designing the subscription program

evals.prompt: A subscriber wants to skip this month's shipment because they have too much product. Should we push them toward a discount to keep them?
evals.expected_output: Should distinguish 'too much product' churn (a cadence problem) from 'don't want this anymore' churn (a genuine save-offer situation), and recommend a skip/pause or cadence-extension prompt rather than a discount for this specific reason. Should explain that a discount save offer for an overstock reason misses the actual fix and burns margin for nothing.
assertions: Distinguishes cadence-related churn from genuine disinterest churn
Recommends skip/pause or cadence adjustment for this specific case, not a discount
Explains why a discount save offer is the wrong tool here
Treats skip as a save mechanism, not a loss

evals.prompt: Our loyalty program members buy way more than non-members. The program is clearly driving huge incremental revenue, right?
evals.expected_output: Should caution against assuming causation from a simple member-vs-non-member comparison — the most engaged customers were likely to join and buy more anyway, regardless of the program. Should recommend a holdout group or before/after cohort comparison to isolate the program's actual incremental lift, referencing the incrementality-checkpoint principle.
assertions: Cautions against assuming the member/non-member gap is fully caused by the program
Explains the self-selection bias (engaged customers join and buy more anyway)
Recommends a holdout or before/after cohort comparison instead
